A Fifth-Floor Window. A congressman.

A Disputed Account.

The death of Marion Zioncheck. The record deserves another reading.

Marion Zioncheck was a U.S. congressman from Washington. His death in Seattle on August 7, 1936 was reported as suicide following a fall from his fifth-floor office.

This project challenges that account. Its collected analyses question the reported movements inside the office, the interpretation of photographs, witness accounts, and the surrounding institutional history.

Five volumes bring together photographs, newspaper reports, personal records, and an argument for re-examining what happened in Seattle on August 7, 1936.

Inquiries of the Record (1–23) live on Pg. 3 · Inquiries.

Marion’s Truth Will Be Heard Project

The morning papers

How the death reached print

The August 8 report in Volume II says Marion re-entered the congressional race to show the public he was neither crazy nor foolish. That explanation makes public appearances part of his response to the image attached to him. The archive also preserves headlines centered on his behavior, while Volume V discusses his planned political speech and conflict with powerful institutions.

The return west

Safe conduct, then the train

The contemporary account reproduced in Volume II describes Kenneth Romney, the House sergeant-at-arms, arranging safe conduct back to Seattle after Marion’s escape from the Maryland institution. It says Capitol police intervened to prevent another arrest, and that Marion ultimately traveled west by train after an airline refused him passage in Chicago.

The photographed note

House stationery, visible creases

Volume II reproduces the handwritten note on House of Representatives stationery, with visible horizontal and vertical creases. Its text concerns an unfair economic system and the chance to survive and live. That political language connects this entry to the dinner speech discussed in Volume V.

Witnesses

Few names, one first story

Volume V places Sol Krems in two roles: a named witness at the scene and the newspaper figure it credits with the first story. It contrasts that named role with references to scores of unnamed witnesses.
